questions.question: How many one-one functions exist from a 3-element set to a 5-element set?
How many onto functions exist from a 4-element set to a 3-element set?
f: A→A where |A|=n is finite, and f is known to be injective. Is f necessarily surjective? Would this still hold if A were infinite (e.g., A = natural numbers)?
questions.solutionApproach: For finite A: yes, injective ⟹ surjective (equal-size shortcut). For infinite A: NOT guaranteed — e.g., f(n)=n+1 on naturals is injective but not surjective (misses 0).
questions.answer: Yes for finite A; NOT guaranteed for infinite A (classic counterexample: f(n)=n+1 on ℕ).

questions.question: Let f(x)=x² on integers. Let A={-2,1}, B={2,-1}. Compute f(A∩B) and f(A)∩f(B). Are they equal?
questions.solutionApproach: A∩B = ∅ (no common elements) so f(A∩B)=∅. f(A)={4,1}, f(B)={4,1}, so f(A)∩f(B)={4,1}. Not equal — demonstrates f(A∩B) ⊆ f(A)∩f(B) can be a STRICT subset when f is not injective.
questions.answer: f(A∩B)=∅, f(A)∩f(B)={4,1} — NOT equal, confirming the general ⊆ (not =) relationship.

questions.question: g∘f is one-one. Must f be one-one? Must g be one-one? Give a counterexample for whichever is NOT guaranteed.
questions.solutionApproach: f MUST be one-one (if f(a1)=f(a2), then g(f(a1))=g(f(a2)), contradicting g∘f one-one unless a1=a2). g need NOT be one-one — counterexample: A={1,2}, B={1,2,3}, C={1,2}, f(1)=1,f(2)=2 (one-one), g(1)=1,g(2)=2,g(3)=1 (not one-one, but g∘f(1)=1,g∘f(2)=2 is one-one).
questions.answer: f must be one-one; g need not be (counterexample above).
